title: Catching the edge of the Phantom Galaxy
caption: The Phantom Galaxy (M74), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: M 74 · constellation Pisces · about 32 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Adamo (Stockholm University) and the FEAST JWST team

recognition.text: Ranked #54 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A large spiral galaxy fills the frame. Its mostly bright white core is circled by swirling structures that resemble water spiralling down a drain, and its rings glow deep red and orange, outlining filaments of dust around cavernous black bubbles. This is M74, the Phantom Galaxy, around 32 million light-years away in Pisces, revisited by Webb.

Dark red traces warm dust threading the galaxy, red shows light re-emitted by complex molecules forming on dust grains, and orange and yellow mark gas ionized by recently formed star clusters. Energy pouring from young stars, called stellar feedback, carves the network of bright knots and black bubbles. Little gas at the center leaves a clear view of the nuclear star cluster.

The data come from the FEAST program, which studies how feedback and star formation interact beyond the Milky Way. The team found that new stars slowly tear apart the gas and dust nurseries where they formed, and that star formation is most active in the spiral arms.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.73 x 1.76 arcminutes) and distance (32 million light years), the frame spans roughly 53,000 × 16,000 light-years. Its light set out about 32 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Dark red and red trace warm dust and complex molecules, orange and yellow gas ionized by young clusters, and blue and cyan the shortest near-infrared wavelengths.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

explore: M74 is a grand design spiral, with prominent, well-defined arms, and it lies almost face-on to Earth, a favorite combination for astronomers studying spiral structure. Webb also maps near-infrared hydrogen emission lines, which are less affected by dust and reveal where massive stars have just formed. ESA/Webb first featured M74 in August 2022.
alt: A large spiral galaxy with a bright white core surrounded by swirling structures, and deep red and orange rings of dust filaments around dark bubbles.
